title: 133 Progeny performance testing as a genetic evaluation of dorper rams for commercially important traits
content:
Abstract
Dorper sheep, a wool-shedding breed that doesn’t require shearing and is historically adapted to harsh and dry environments, is growing in popularity in semi-arid regions of the United States, including West Texas. Dorper are also known to produce a desirable carcass particularly valued in expanding non-traditional marketing channels. However, compared to beef and dairy cattle and other sheep-breeds such Katahdin and Polypay, there has been limited adoption of technology by industry stakeholders to genetically evaluate Dorper sheep for hard-to-measure traits such as parasite resistance, growth, and carcass value. The purpose of this trial is to perform a genetic evaluation of industry rams from reputable breeders for commercially relevant traits by performance testing their progeny groups in a singular environment. The objective of this project is to determine baseline genetic information for multiple flocks, develop a bank of genotypic and phenotypic records for future genomics research, and promote the use of technology, such as quantitative genetic selection and genomics, that can improve current selection practices. In year one of this three-year trial, 7 rams were sourced from 6 different stakeholder flocks and mated to a single Dorper flock maintained by Texas A&M AgriLife in San Angelo, TX. Rams were group mated in a large pasture (500 acres) setting with 107 resulting progeny being produced. Progeny in each of the sire groups varied from 4 to 34 lambs. Lambs were managed as a single cohort on pasture through a post weaning phase for 75 days, and then put in a dry lot pen and provided ab-libitum access to a total-mixed ration designed for growing lambs (~14% crude protein). To quantify parasite resistance during the feeding phase, lambs were experimentally infected with 10,000 L3 Haemonchus contortus larvae and subsequent fecal egg counts and packed-cell volumes were collected. Finally, wether lambs (N = 36) were harvested with a variety of carcass quality and quantity measurements collected. Analyses of sire group performance data was conducted using Proc Glimmix in SAS (v9.4) with model corrections for litter size, lamb sex and dam age. Significant differences (P ≤ 0.05) between the sire group averages were observed for fecal egg count (FEC) following experimental infection (range = 1,026 – 2,316 eggs per gram), loineye area (range = 16.58 - 21.49 cm2) and backfat depth (range = 0.46 – 1.0 cm). A trending difference (P ≤ 0.1) was identified for post-weaning average daily gain. Results from year one suggest that a sire testing protocol is suitable for identifying genetic differences in commercially important traits between the tested sires. These preliminary results will be expanded in future years of this study to develop a baseline of genetic information foundational for enhanced genetic selection in this expanding breed.
